account: A male infant was delivered at an outside hospital at 34 weeks and 2 days. Both kidneys were enlarged with innumerable tiny cysts, consistent with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. He was cared for in the Mount Sinai neonatal intensive care unit in New York and died at two days of life. Whole-genome sequencing found a known pathogenic missense variant from his father. SpliceAI scores in the NICUnet Rareservoir then identified a maternally inherited deep intronic PKHD1 variant scoring 0.98. RNA studies on kidney epithelial cells derived from his mother's urine confirmed that the variant creates a novel exon with a premature stop codon. The laboratory GeneDx classified it as likely pathogenic. After genetic counseling, the parents proceeded with in vitro fertilization (IVF) and preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders within one year of the death. The case report was published online on 10 January 2024. Its authors write that splicing algorithms had until then been used in retrospective research. They write that such algorithms had not been used as a first step in clinical practice. In 2025 an Israeli team reported that a common deep intronic PKHD1 variant in Bedouin families received the lowest and most benign scores across splicing prediction tools among all known PKHD1 splicing variants. In 2026 a team in the Philippines and Japan used SpliceAI the same way to find a deep intronic IFT172 variant in a boy with nephronophthisis.

ai_role.statement: SpliceAI's score of 0.98 nominated the maternally inherited deep intronic variant as the second allele. Among 78,575 rare intronic PKHD1 variants in gnomAD only one scored higher. Pathogenicity was then established by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing of maternal urine-derived cells and GeneDx's likely-pathogenic classification. The AI's contribution was candidate selection. Without it the second allele would have remained unexplained. Authors declare no relevant financial interests.

Both kidneys were enlarged with innumerable tiny cysts, consistent with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. He was cared for in the Mount Sinai neonatal intensive care unit in New York and died at two days of life. Whole-genome sequencing found a known pathogenic missense variant from his father. SpliceAI scores in the NICUnet Rareservoir then identified a maternally inherited deep intronic PKHD1 variant scoring 0.98. RNA studies on kidney epithelial cells derived from his mother's urine confirmed that the variant creates a novel exon with a premature stop codon. The laboratory GeneDx classified it as likely pathogenic. After genetic counseling, the parents proceeded with in vitro fertilization (IVF) and preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders within one year of the death. The case report was published online on 10 January 2024. Its authors write that splicing algorithms had until then been used in retrospective research. They write that such algorithms had not been used as a first step in clinical practice. In 2025 an Israeli team reported that a common deep intronic PKHD1 variant in Bedouin families received the lowest and most benign scores across splicing prediction tools among all known PKHD1 splicing variants. In 2026 a team in the Philippines and Japan used SpliceAI the same way to find a deep intronic IFT172 variant in a boy with nephronophthisis.
fields.summary: SpliceAI scored a hidden PKHD1 variant at 0.98, and after RNA studies confirmed it, the parents of the infant who died used the diagnosis to plan IVF with embryo genetic testing.

purpose: SpliceAI is a deep-learning model built to predict the effect of DNA variants on RNA splicing. Nominating a splice-altering deep intronic variant is exactly its intended use.

ratings.reason: An identifiable family received a definitive molecular cause of their son's death. They used it for IVF with preimplantation genetic testing to avoid a recurrence of the lethal disease. The infant himself died at two days of life.
